Topic Modeling Short Feedback Messages

Source: vignettes/math_vignette.Rmd
math_vignette.Rmd

sbert computes Sentence-BERT embeddings natively in R. Sentence-BERT (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) is a family of neural models that turn a whole sentence or short text into an embedding: a vector of numbers in which texts with similar meaning lie close together, even when they share few words. sbert downloads a pinned, hash-verified model, tokenizes text with the model’s own Hugging Face tokenizer, runs the model through ONNX Runtime, and pools and normalizes the result in base R. On top of the embeddings it fits topic models: texts whose embeddings are close are grouped into a topic, so a topic is defined by what its texts mean rather than by the words they share.

The feedback_translations dataset included in the sbert package comprises 8,757 AI-generated feedback messages originating from a mathematics learning application and translated into English from ten source languages. Given the size of the corpus and the substantial repetition among messages, manual inspection is impractical. Moreover, conventional frequency-based analyses provide limited insight into the underlying content, as they primarily capture recurring linguistic templates rather than the semantic structure of the feedback. For example, the most frequent message, “Try again.”, occurs 11 times. Topic modeling offers a systematic approach to identifying the principal types of feedback generated by the application and quantifying their relative prevalence.

To ensure methodological transparency and reproducibility, all analytical procedures are designed to be deterministic, such that repeated execution of the document yields identical numerical results, visualizations, and textual outputs under the specified computational environment.

The analysis proceeds in three stages, beginning with data-driven topic-number selection, followed by the construction of a six-topic model and a systematic evaluation of its results from three complementary perspectives:

  1. Model quality assessment. Topic coherence and topic diversity are evaluated to assess the semantic interpretability and distinctiveness of the identified topics prior to substantive interpretation.
  2. Comparative keyword analysis. Two complementary keyword representations are examined for each topic: raw within-topic term frequencies, which identify the most prevalent vocabulary, and class-based term frequency–inverse class frequency (c-TF-IDF), which identifies terms that are particularly distinctive of a given topic relative to the remaining corpus. Comparing these representations makes it possible to distinguish generally frequent expressions from vocabulary that is specifically characteristic of individual topics. Differences between the two rankings are also considered analytically informative.
  3. Representative message analysis. For each topic, representative messages are selected according to their proximity to the corresponding topic centroid in the embedding space. These examples provide interpretable, document-level evidence for the semantic characterization of each topic and enable the proposed topic labels to be evaluated against the original feedback content.

Together, these procedures provide a reproducible and interpretable characterization of the feedback generated by the application, combining quantitative measures of model quality with lexical evidence and representative textual examples.

The vignette builds offline. The embeddings of the 600 messages used here are stored in the package, so no model is downloaded while it is built. When you run the code yourself, the model is downloaded once (about 90 MB) and you get the same results.

The data

Many messages repeat word for word. “Try again.” alone occurs 11 times. dedupe() keeps one copy of each distinct message and records in n how often it occurred. To keep the vignette fast we use the first 600 distinct messages; remove head() to model all of them.

corpus <- head(dedupe(feedback_translations$translation), 600)
head(corpus)
#>                                                                        text n
#> 1                                        Do you know what “one more” means? 2
#> 2                     There should be two more in the red than in the blue. 3
#> 3                                   If it’s not a person, what could it be? 2
#> 4                            What does “everyone after the first one” mean? 1
#> 5 There are five pictures in the gray box. Where is there one picture less? 2
#> 6                                            How do the pictures alternate? 1

The sentence model

models() lists the 14 models that sbert can download. Each is pinned to one fixed version and checked against a SHA-256 hash when it is downloaded.

The default, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, is a small English sentence model that turns a text of up to 256 tokens into 384 numbers. Download it once:

model_download()

topics() and compare_topics() call encode() for you, so the embeddings never have to be handled by hand.

Choosing the number of topics

There is no correct number of topics. compare_topics() fits one model for each candidate count and reports three measures for each:

  • explained: the share of the variation in the embeddings that the topics capture. It grows with every added topic, so it cannot choose the count on its own.
  • coherence: whether each topic’s top words appear together in the same messages (NPMI, from −1 to 1; higher is better).
  • topic_diversity: the number of distinct words in the topics’ top-10 lists, divided by the length of all the lists together. It is 1 when no two topics share a top word.

Only explained is computed from the embeddings. Coherence and diversity are computed from words, so they are a rough guide. The real test of a count is whether each topic’s messages say the same thing, which the next sections check.

sweep <- compare_topics(
  corpus,
  column = "text",
  n_topics = c(4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12)
)
sweep
#> <sbert_topic_sweep> 7 candidates, coherence measure: npmi
#>  n_topics  coherence topic_diversity explained
#>         4 -0.2070855       0.9250000 0.1229819
#>         5 -0.1860037       0.9400000 0.1839887
#>         6 -0.1044246       0.9166667 0.2255144
#>         7 -0.1894843       0.9142857 0.2355033
#>         8 -0.1181287       0.9000000 0.2433832
#>        10 -0.1866628       0.8600000 0.2563262
#>        12 -0.2138928       0.8151261 0.2716759
#> 
#> Fitted models retained: fitted(x, n_topics = 6)
plot(sweep)

Coherence is negative at every count, because the messages are short and two words rarely occur in the same message. It is highest at six topics (−0.10), with eight close behind (−0.12). We use six. fitted() returns the six-topic model that compare_topics() already fitted, so nothing is refitted:

topic_model <- fitted(sweep, n_topics = 6)
topic_model
#> <sbert_topic_model>
#>   documents: 600 
#>   topics: 6
#>   model: precomputed embeddings
#>   algorithm: deterministic k-means (Lloyd)
#>   topic sizes: 223, 133, 131, 49, 37, 27
#>   between/total SS: 22.6%

The topics

topic_sizes() lists the topics. The label of each topic is the message closest to the topic’s center, cut at 60 characters, and n_documents counts its messages:

topic_sizes(topic_model)
#>   topic                                                       label n_documents
#> 1     1   Where is the cow and the cake? Choose all the pictures...         223
#> 2     2            All the ones between the cat and the strawberry.         133
#> 3     3         What does “all the ones between the leaf and the...         131
#> 4     4 Are you sure you have fewer pictures in the red box than...          49
#> 5     5      In the top middle box, it means something is in the...          37
#> 6     6    It is not a person, does not have a hat, and is sitting.          27
#>   proportion
#> 1 0.37166667
#> 2 0.22166667
#> 3 0.21833333
#> 4 0.08166667
#> 5 0.06166667
#> 6 0.04500000

Reading the label and the messages of each topic shows that the topics are not subjects but kinds of feedback: what the message does for the learner.

  1. Guiding question and instruction. A question that makes the learner find something, followed by an order to act on it: Where is the cow and the cake? Choose all the pictures that are between them.
  2. Short hint. A fragment with no verb that restates the target: All the ones between the cat and the strawberry.
  3. Question about meaning. A question that asks the learner what a phrase means: What does “all the ones between the leaf and the unicorn” mean?
  4. Correction. A statement of what should be true, or a question that makes the learner check their answer: There should be two fewer in the red one than in the blue one. Are you sure you have fewer pictures in the red box than in the blue one?
  5. Definition. An explanation of what a word or phrase means: “Sitting” means your bottom is on the ground or on a chair.
  6. Negation. A description built from what something is not, used to rule out answers: It is not a person, does not have a hat, and is sitting. If it’s an animal, then it’s not a person.

Topics 1, 2, and 3 are about the same exercise, finding the pictures between two others, and use the same words. The model still separates them, because an instruction, a hint, and a question do different things. Topics 3 and 5 both deal with meaning, but one asks the learner and the other tells them.

name_topics() gives the topics these names, one per topic in topic order. The names replace the labels in every table and plot that follows; nothing is refitted.

topic_model <- name_topics(
  topic_model,
  c(
    "Guiding question and instruction",
    "Short hint",
    "Question about meaning",
    "Correction",
    "Definition",
    "Negation"
  )
)
topic_sizes(topic_model)
#>   topic                            label n_documents proportion
#> 1     1 Guiding question and instruction         223 0.37166667
#> 2     2                       Short hint         133 0.22166667
#> 3     3           Question about meaning         131 0.21833333
#> 4     4                       Correction          49 0.08166667
#> 5     5                       Definition          37 0.06166667
#> 6     6                         Negation          27 0.04500000

Example messages

A few messages per topic show its range. representatives() returns the messages closest to each topic’s center; the first message of each topic is the one that labeled it before we named it:

knitr::kable(
  representatives(topic_model, n = 3, rank = "distance"),
  digits = 2
)
topic rank document_id text distance margin
1 1 118 Where is the cow and the cake? Choose all the pictures that are between them. 0.20 0.28
1 2 474 Where is the second and the fourth picture? Choose the pictures that are between them. 0.22 0.19
1 3 368 Do you know where the first picture is? Choose all the pictures that come after it. 0.23 0.21
2 1 277 All the ones between the cat and the strawberry. 0.17 0.28
2 2 237 All the ones between the piglet and the dog. 0.18 0.30
2 3 226 All the ones between the leaf and the unicorn. 0.18 0.23
3 1 227 What does “all the ones between the leaf and the unicorn” mean? 0.18 0.29
3 2 87 What does “all the ones between the dog and the strawberry” mean? 0.19 0.29
3 3 479 What does “all the ones between the chestnut and the deer” mean? 0.23 0.29
4 1 218 Are you sure you have fewer pictures in the red box than in the blue one? 0.14 0.46
4 2 62 It’s not enough to just have more—there must be exactly two more pictures in the red box than in the blue box. 0.15 0.48
4 3 68 Are you sure you have two more pictures in the blue box than in the red box? 0.17 0.40
5 1 364 In the top middle box, it means something is in the middle at the top. 0.29 0.16
5 2 28 Do you know what “at the top in the middle” means? 0.32 0.15
5 3 74 What does it mean to be on the grass? 0.33 0.23
6 1 366 It is not a person, does not have a hat, and is sitting. 0.16 0.50
6 2 31 It’s not a person, it has a hat, and it’s sitting. 0.16 0.47
6 3 18 It’s a person, has a hat, and isn’t standing. 0.17 0.42

distance is the cosine distance from the message to the topic’s center: the smaller, the more typical. margin is how much farther the message is from the next closest topic: the larger, the more clearly it belongs to its own. The default, rank = "margin", ranks by margin instead, which favors messages that could belong to no other topic.

The plot shows the same messages, with the similarity to the center in parentheses:

plot(topic_model, type = "representatives", n_representatives = 3)

Topic sizes

n_documents counts distinct messages. Because we removed duplicates, a message that was shown 11 times counts once. Passing the counts as weights adds n_weighted and weighted_share, which count every time a message was shown.

topic_sizes(topic_model, weights = corpus$n)
#>   topic                            label n_documents proportion n_weighted
#> 1     1 Guiding question and instruction         223 0.37166667        267
#> 2     2                       Short hint         133 0.22166667        162
#> 3     3           Question about meaning         131 0.21833333        138
#> 4     4                       Correction          49 0.08166667         76
#> 5     5                       Definition          37 0.06166667         57
#> 6     6                         Negation          27 0.04500000         40
#>   weighted_share
#> 1     0.36081081
#> 2     0.21891892
#> 3     0.18648649
#> 4     0.10270270
#> 5     0.07702703
#> 6     0.05405405

Corrections (topic 4) grow from 8.2% of the distinct messages to 10.3% of all messages shown, so the app repeated its corrections more often than its other kinds of feedback.

plot(topic_model, type = "sizes")

The words each topic uses

Words do not define a topic here; the sentences do. Still, the words a topic uses more than the others can be useful, for example to search the messages or to see how a topic is phrased. terms() lists them. The score is class-based TF-IDF: it is high for words that are frequent in this topic and rare in the others.

terms(topic_model, n = 5)

plot(topic_model, type = "terms")

The words show why they make poor names. They describe what the messages are about, not what they do. Topic 2’s top words, after ones, are names of pictures (broccoli, candy, hippo) that change from message to message, and nothing in them says that the topic is made of short hints. Topic 6’s words (person, animal, hat) name the pictures, not the negation that defines the topic. And topics 2 and 3 share the word ones, although one gives a hint and the other asks a question.

summary() adds the coherence of each topic’s top words. It is lowest for topic 2 and highest for topic 4, whose messages repeat the same few words (box, red, blue):

summary(topic_model)
#> Semantic topic model summary
#>   documents:            600
#>   topics:               6
#>   model:                precomputed embeddings
#>   between/total SS:      22.6%
#>   mean npmi  coherence:  -0.1044
#>   topic topic_diversity:      0.917 (top 10 terms)
#> 
#>  topic                            label n_documents proportion coherence
#>      1 Guiding question and instruction         223    0.37167   -0.2368
#>      2                       Short hint         133    0.22167   -0.4150
#>      3           Question about meaning         131    0.21833   -0.2564
#>      4                       Correction          49    0.08167    0.3011
#>      5                       Definition          37    0.06167   -0.2043
#>      6                         Negation          27    0.04500    0.1849

To name topics by their three top words instead of a sentence, fit with label = "terms".

Everything in one figure

type = "fit" shows each topic’s example messages and, beside them, its words, one row per topic:

plot(topic_model, type = "fit", n_terms = 8, n_representatives = 3)

Next steps

  • predict(topic_model, new_text) assigns new messages to these topics without refitting.
  • topic_membership(topic_model) gives each message a probability for every topic instead of a single topic.
  • segment = "sentence" in topics() or compare_topics() splits each message into sentences and models the sentences. topic_gamma() then gives the mix of topics in each message.
  • topic_corpus() encodes the text once so that you can fit many models without encoding again.
  • To model the original messages in their ten source languages, use topics(feedback_translations, column = "feedback", n_topics = 6, model = "paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2").

The article Topic Modeling COVID-19 Research Abstracts on the package website works through a larger corpus of long research abstracts.
